name: ESP32 Marauder v8
firmware_note: The official Marauder firmware on the official v8 board. Same MIT-licensed firmware that runs on ~25 other boards; the v8 exists to give it a battery, touchscreen, GPS, SD and two SMA antennas.
price_note: Sold out at the vendor as of 2026-09-06. Battery is NOT included - you supply a 3.7V 18650. Add ~$8 for the cell and ~$8 for a microSD, so realistically ~$116 all-in.
skill_note: Touchscreen menu, no command line needed for the common functions; it arrives flashed and working.
build_note: Ships assembled in a 3D-printed enclosure. You add an 18650 cell and a microSD card yourself.
summary: The current flagship official Marauder board: an ESP32-C5 with a 2.8-inch touchscreen, GPS, microSD and dual SMA antenna connectors. The C5 makes it the first Marauder that can see and transmit on 5 GHz as well as 2.4 GHz. It is a Wi-Fi and BLE analysis and attack tool, and nothing else.
honest_take: This is a Wi-Fi/BLE box, not a Flipper competitor - there is no sub-GHz, no NFC, no RFID and no IR, so the ~30% of Flipper use cases that involve gates, badges and TV remotes are simply absent. Its headline deauth attack only works against unprotected management frames: 802.11w/PMF stops it dead, and WPA3 makes PMF mandatory, so on any modern network deauth increasingly does nothing. The firmware is free and MIT-licensed and runs on a $20 M5StickC Plus2, so what you are paying $100 for is the C5's 5 GHz radio, the touchscreen, the GPS and the antenna connectors - which is a fair deal, but understand that is what you are buying.
best_for: Wi-Fi site survey and channel analysis across both bands
Wardriving with GPS and Wigle-compatible logging
Detecting BLE trackers, Flipper Zeros and Flock Safety cameras
not_for: Sub-GHz, NFC, RFID or IR work - it has none of that hardware
Deauthing WPA3 or any PMF-enabled network
Cracking Wi-Fi passwords on-device - it captures handshakes, your laptop cracks them
Bluetooth Classic work - the C5 is BLE-only

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Single-core 32-bit RISC-V up to 240MHz. The only Espressif part with dual-band 2.4+5GHz Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax, a/b/g/n/ac backward compatible). 384KB SRAM plus external PSRAM.

radios.note: Dual-band 2.4GHz + 5GHz Wi-Fi 6. Marauder's configs.h sets HAS_DUAL_BAND for this board and drops channel hop delay from 1000ms to 250ms.
Bluetooth 5 LE only. No Bluetooth Classic / BR/EDR on any C5.

hardware.battery_note: Takes a user-supplied 3.7V 18650 flat-top cell; not included. Onboard LiPo charging circuit and on-screen fuel gauge.
hardware.storage: microSD slot, used for pcap capture and firmware updates
notable_physical: Dual female SMA connectors for Wi-Fi and GPS antennas

wifi_scan_24.note: AP, station, probe-request and raw sniffing; channel analyzer and packet-rate graphing

wifi_scan_5.note: ESP32-C5 dual-band radio; HAS_DUAL_BAND set for this board in configs.h

wifi_monitor_mode.note: ESP-IDF promiscuous mode; raw capture written to SD as pcap

wifi_injection.note: Raw 802.11 frame TX via esp_wifi_80211_tx. Fine for management frames (deauth, beacon, CSA); not general-purpose injection like an Atheros adapter

wifi_deauth_24.note: Broadcast, targeted and manual modes. Only works where management frames are unprotected - 802.11w/PMF defeats it entirely

wifi_deauth_5.note: The C5 can transmit on 5GHz, but 5GHz deauth is new and far less tested than the 2.4GHz path. Same PMF limitation applies

wifi_evil_twin.note: WIFI_SCAN_EVIL_PORTAL - clones a scanned SSID and serves a captive portal

wifi_captive_portal.note: EvilPortal module, HTML served from SD card, credentials logged to SD

wifi_handshake_capture.note: Passive and active EAPOL capture (WIFI_SCAN_EAPOL / ACTIVE_EAPOL), saved as pcap. Cracking happens off-device

wifi_pmkid.note: EAPOL capture is explicit in the source; a dedicated PMKID mode is not. Could not confirm

wifi_beacon_spam.note: Random, list-based, rickroll and 'funny' beacon spam modes

wifi_probe_sniff.note: WIFI_SCAN_PROBE - logs probe requests and the SSIDs clients are looking for

wifi_wardriving.note: Wi-Fi, station and BLE wardrive modes with GPS tagging, Wigle-compatible CSV to SD

ble_scan.note: NimBLE-based; general scan plus analyzer and signal-strength fox hunt

ble_advertise.note: Used by all the spam and AirTag-spoof modes

ble_spam_apple.note: BT_ATTACK_SOUR_APPLE and BT_ATTACK_APPLE_JUICE. Apple has hardened against this since 2023; effectiveness varies by iOS version

bt_classic.note: Notable absence. ESP32-C5 is Bluetooth 5 LE only - no BR/EDR. No classic inquiry scans or legacy pairing work

ble_sniff.note: It observes advertisements, which is what every ESP32 'BLE sniffer' really does. It cannot follow a connection across channel hops like a dedicated sniffer

ble_tracker_detect.note: BT_SCAN_AIRTAG and AIRTAG_MON - matches Apple Find My advertisement payloads

findmy_track.note: BT_FINDMY_SOUND and BT_ATTACK_FINDMY_LIVE interact with Find My accessories; not a tracking network client

detect_flipper.note: BT_SCAN_FLIPPER - matches the Flipper Zero's BLE advertisement name/pattern. Trivially defeated by renaming the Flipper

detect_airtag.note: Matches Apple Find My BLE advertisement type

detect_skimmer.note: BT_SCAN_SKIMMERS - matches known credit-card-skimmer BLE module names (HC-05 style) and default pairing patterns, not skimmers as such

detect_pineapple.note: WIFI_SCAN_PINESCAN - flags one BSSID advertising many SSIDs, the PineAP/KARMA signature

detect_pwnagotchi.note: WIFI_SCAN_PWN - matches the pwnagotchi beacon advertisement

detect_surveillance_cam.note: BT_SCAN_FLOCK and BT_SCAN_FLOCK_WARDRIVE match the BLE signature of Flock Safety ALPR cameras specifically. BT_SCAN_RAYBAN matches Meta Ray-Ban glasses. Not a general camera detector

gps.note: Onboard multi-constellation module with ceramic antenna, SMA-upgradeable

sd_logging.note: pcap, wardrive CSV and captured portal credentials

scriptable.note: Serial/CLI command interface drivable from a PC or Android; no on-device scripting language

standalone_untethered.note: Battery, touchscreen and SD - fully usable with no host

subghz_rx.note: Notable absence. No sub-GHz radio of any kind. Cannot touch garage doors, gates or key fobs

ir_tx.note: No IR emitter on this board

usb_hid_inject.note: The Marauder firmware implements no HID/BadUSB function on this board

legal.notes: Owning and using it to scan and log is legal in most places. Transmitting deauthentication frames against networks you do not own is a separate matter - the US FCC has fined hotel and conference operators for Wi-Fi deauth blocking, and equivalent computer-misuse laws apply in most countries. The captive-portal feature collects other people's credentials, which is where casual use turns into a criminal offence fastest. Check your local law.

ecosystem.app_store: No - single monolithic firmware, but a web-based Marauder Installer and a Flipper Zero companion app exist

name: ESP32 Marauder Mini v3
firmware_note: Same official Marauder firmware as the v8, built for the Mini v3 target. Also dual-band via ESP32-C5, but with a small screen and no touch.
price_note: Stock fluctuates - listed in stock on the storefront and sold out on the product page on the same day (2026-09-06). Battery NOT included (vendor suggests a 3.7V 820mAh 653042 cell, ~$8) and no microSD included, so ~$110 all-in.
skill_note: 5-way tactile switch menu; arrives flashed. Smaller screen makes the denser views harder to read than the v8.
build_note: Ships assembled with a 3D-printed enclosure. You add a LiPo cell (watch the polarity - the vendor warns wrong polarity damages the charge circuit) and a microSD.
summary: The pocket-sized official Marauder. Same ESP32-C5 dual-band radio and same firmware as the v8, in a roughly 2.5 x 1.5 inch package with a small screen, 5-way switch, GPS and microSD. Aimed at being carried every day rather than sat on a bench.
honest_take: It is the v8's radio and firmware minus the touchscreen and minus the 18650, for $5 less - the value is the form factor, not the capability. The same caveats bite harder here: no sub-GHz, no NFC, no IR, and deauth that 802.11w/PMF and therefore WPA3 defeats outright. The tiny screen makes the channel analyser and packet views genuinely cramped, and with no battery in the box it is not actually pocketable until you buy one.
best_for: GPS wardriving in a jacket pocket
Spotting BLE trackers and Flipper Zeros while walking around
not_for: Reading dense packet views - the screen is small
Long sessions - it takes a small ~820mAh cell

name: ESP32 Marauder v7
firmware_note: Still a first-class firmware target - v1.15.1 ships a marauder_v7.bin - even though the board itself is no longer sold. 2.4GHz only.
price_note: No longer listed in the vendor's catalogue as of 2026-09-06; superseded by the v8 and Mini v3. Secondhand only, and prices there are not a reliable figure to quote.
build_note: Shipped assembled. Firmware updates still supported via the web installer.
summary: The generation before the v8: an ESP32 with a full screen, a small physical keyboard, battery, GPS, SD and a temperature sensor. It is 2.4GHz only - the dual-band C5 did not arrive until the v8 and Mini v3. Still fully supported by current firmware.
honest_take: Buying one secondhand today means paying for a board whose radio is a generation behind, and the 5 GHz gap is the one that actually matters now that most real networks have a 5 GHz side the v7 cannot even see. It is not obsolete - the firmware still gets releases - but a $20 M5StickC Plus2 runs the same 2.4GHz feature set, so the v7's value is the keyboard, the GPS and the battery rather than anything the radio does.
best_for: 2.4GHz Wi-Fi and BLE work where the keyboard is genuinely useful
GPS wardriving on a budget if you already own one
not_for: Anything on 5 GHz - the radio cannot see it

hardware.mcu_primary_note: An ESP32-family part, 2.4GHz only (configs.h does not set HAS_DUAL_BAND for MARAUDER_V7). The vendor never published the exact part number and the board is no longer listed, so it is left null rather than guessed.

name: ESP32 Marauder v6.1
firmware_note: Older official board, still a maintained firmware target (v6_1.bin ships with v1.15.1). Touchscreen, 2.4GHz only.
price_note: Out of the vendor's catalogue as of 2026-09-06. Secondhand prices vary too widely to quote as a figure.
build_note: Shipped assembled; still updatable through the web installer.
summary: The touchscreen Marauder that preceded the v7 and v8. ESP32, 2.4GHz only, with a touch display, IP5306-based battery management, buttons, a NeoPixel, microSD, GPS and a temperature sensor. The v6.1 added GPS over the plain v6.
honest_take: Two generations old and 2.4GHz only, which is the limitation that matters most today. The firmware still supports it, so it is not e-waste, but there is no reason to seek one out - the same firmware runs on a $20 M5StickC Plus2 with the same radio capability, and a current v8 adds 5 GHz that no amount of firmware can retrofit onto this board.
best_for: Owners who already have one - it still gets current firmware
Learning 802.11 on 2.4GHz with a touchscreen UI
not_for: Buying today - discontinued and superseded twice over

name: M5StickC Plus2 (ESP32 Marauder)
firmware_note: The same official Marauder firmware flashed onto a stock $20 M5Stack dev kit. This is the cheapest legitimate way to run Marauder, and it is why the official boards have to justify themselves on hardware rather than software.
price_note: M5Stack has marked the StickC Plus2 EOL and it is out of stock as of 2026-09-06; the shop points buyers at the M5StickS3 ($21.50) instead. The Plus2 is still the last Stick with Bluetooth Classic, which is why people still hunt for it.
skill_note: You flash it yourself - the web installer makes this a few minutes, but nothing arrives working and there is no support if it goes wrong.
build_note: Buy the dev kit, flash the m5stickc_plus2 binary with the browser-based Marauder Installer. No soldering. Adding SD card storage requires building an adapter onto the front pin header.
summary: A stock M5Stack M5StickC Plus2 dev kit running the official ESP32 Marauder firmware. Roughly $20 buys you most of the Marauder Wi-Fi and BLE feature set in a 48 x 24 mm package with a 1.14-inch screen and a 200 mAh battery. It is the reference point every purpose-built ESP32 security gadget should be measured against.
honest_take: This is the honest baseline for the whole category: the firmware is free and MIT-licensed, so a $20 dev kit gives you the same 2.4GHz Wi-Fi and BLE attacks as a $100 purpose-built board. What you give up is real though - no SD card slot means no sustained pcap capture, the 200 mAh battery gives well under an hour with the radio busy, there is no GPS so no wardriving, and no external antenna connector. And it is 2.4GHz only, so no 5 GHz, plus deauth that PMF and WPA3 defeat. Worth knowing it is now EOL at M5Stack, and that it is the only board here with Bluetooth Classic - the ESP32-S3 successors are all BLE-only.
best_for: Learning what Marauder actually does before spending real money
Bluetooth Classic work, which the S3-based successors cannot do at all
not_for: Packet capture - there is no SD card slot
Any session longer than about an hour - 200 mAh
USB HID/BadUSB - no native USB, only a CH9102 bridge

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Xtensa dual-core ESP32 (ECO V3) up to 240MHz, 8MB flash, 2MB Quad PSRAM in a SiP package.

radios.note: Bluetooth v4.2 BR/EDR (Classic) AND Bluetooth LE - the only board in this batch with Classic

wifi_deauth_24.note: Defeated by 802.11w/PMF and therefore by WPA3

wifi_handshake_capture.note: EAPOL capture runs, but with no SD card there is no practical place to store pcaps

wifi_wardriving.note: No GPS and no SD - the two things wardriving needs

packet_capture.note: No SD slot as shipped; requires a hand-built adapter on the front header

detect_skimmer.note: Matches known skimmer BLE module naming patterns

sd_logging.note: Requires hand-building an SD adapter onto the 8-pin front header

legal.notes: The hardware is a generic IoT dev kit and is unrestricted everywhere. The legal exposure comes entirely from what you flash onto it and point it at: deauthing networks you do not own and running credential-harvesting portals are offences in most jurisdictions regardless of how cheap the hardware was. Check your local law.
